library(icorp26)

Assignment 3 asks you to do the following things:


1.  Run four T-Tests: for two different populations and two different ‘comparison’ groups (N=4).  

2. Using SPSS or R, graphically display them on a well-labeled barchart, including significance levels
Write a RQ and Findings for each.  


The first thing that you need to do is to decide on your
variables and these fall into two groups:

1. Outcome variables
2. Variables defining groups.


Because Prof. Battle asked you to do t tests which reuire means, the outcome
variables must be appropriate for calculating a mean.
That means that they should be _numeric_ also known as _interval_.
However, it is sometimes okay to treat _ordinal_ variables
as though they are numbers.  This is probably what you will
need to do.




As an example let's use variables from rss7. You need to pick different
variables.


*Make a list of your outcome variables here*


*Make a list of your 2 populations*

By populations he means a subgroup of the sample that you
will study.  
For example:
Men
People who live in the Southeast.
Hispanic people.
Straight people.
Elderly people.

That is to say, the population is one category of one 
variable. 

*Make a list of your group variables here*

You need (at least) two grouping variables. These 
will define groups within your population that you will compare.
Thinking back to assignment two you can use some of the 
same variables.

For the example I will use:
Outcome:
For the examples we'll use `rss1$SUN_CLOUDY` convert to
numeric (I can reuse my old code).


```{r}
rss1$SUN_CLOUDY_N <- to_numeric(rss1$SUN_CLOUDY)

```
For my two populations I will use :

1. Hispanic people (`P_RACE_R`).
2. People over age 70 (`P_AGEC_R == "70+"`).

For my comparisons I will use: gender (`P_GENDER`) 
and language used with doctor (`LAN_DOCTOR`).

Also note that we have access to _all_ of the RSS data sets.
Use the one that has the variables you are interested in.

The first step is that we will create two new data sets, one
with only Hispanics and one with only people over 70.
Again, you can look at assignment 2 and follow the same model.

```{r}
data_filter(rss1, P_AGEC_R == "70+") -> older
data_filter(rss1, P_RACE_R  == "Hispanic") -> hispanic 
```
*What are your sample sizes?*


I had this in assignment 2 but let's look at the basic results.

```{r}
datawizard::means_by_group(hispanic$SUN_CLOUDY_N,
                           hispanic$LAN_DOCTOR) 
datawizard::means_by_group(hispanic$SUN_CLOUDY_N,
                           hispanic$P_GENDER)
```

```{r}
datawizard::means_by_group(older$SUN_CLOUDY_N,
                           older$LAN_DOCTOR)
datawizard::means_by_group(older$SUN_CLOUDY_N,
                           older$P_GENDER)
```

Now, Prof. Battle asked for t tests. These results
don't give us t-tests. However, they do give us F tests. 
So before we go to t tests, it's important to say that 
the "p values" will be more or less the same as for F tests.

That is, if you look at the p values and they are < .050 by
convention you can say that the relationships are statistically
significant or that can _reject the null hypothesis_ that there 
are no differences between the means. If you look over the 
sample results 3 of the 4 null hypotheses can be rejected. 

*Which one cannot be rejected?*

(Please see the separate article about statistical significance
and effect size.)
https://elinw.github.io/icorp26/articles/two_variables.html 
which looks at yet another test, the Chi Square.

## T Tests

T tests are very specific in that we can only compare two
means.  This is a problem for the analysis because `LAN_DOCTOR`
has three possible values. Look at your variables. Do they have more than
two categories?  
Let's remove people who speak
"Another language" with their doctors.  
This means we do another filter.

`!=` mean `not equal`. 

If you need to do this step, the easiest mistake is to 
misspell the variable name or put in capitals where there
should be lower case letters.
```{r}
data_filter(hispanic, LAN_DOCTOR != "Another language") -> hispanic
data_filter(older, LAN_DOCTOR != "Another language") -> older 
```
(There are other ways we could have handled this problem!)

*If you had to do this, how did your two sample sizes change?



We also have to do one other weird R thing, to tell
the system that no there are only two values for LAN_DOCTOR.

```{r}
hispanic$LAN_DOCTOR_releveled <-droplevels(hispanic$LAN_DOCTOR,)
```
```{r}
older$LAN_DOCTOR_releveled <- droplevels(older$LAN_DOCTOR)
```


Now let's do a t test in R. 

```{r}
t.test(SUN_CLOUDY_N ~ P_GENDER, data = hispanic)
```

```{r}
t.test(SUN_CLOUDY_N ~ LAN_DOCTOR_releveled, data = hispanic)
```

```{r}
t.test(SUN_CLOUDY_N ~ P_GENDER, data = older)
```

```{r}
t.test(SUN_CLOUDY_N ~ LAN_DOCTOR_releveled, data = older)
```
*How do these results compare to the F tests?*


Let's try the F Tests again, remembering that we removed
people from the sample!



Last step, we can make our plots. They will also give the 
F test results.

```{r}

datawizard::means_by_group(hispanic$SUN_CLOUDY_N,
                           hispanic$LAN_DOCTOR_releveled) |>
                plot()
datawizard::means_by_group(hispanic$SUN_CLOUDY_N,
                           hispanic$P_GENDER) |>
                plot()
```

```{r}
datawizard::means_by_group(older$SUN_CLOUDY_N,
                           older$LAN_DOCTOR_releveled) |>
     plot()
datawizard::means_by_group(older$SUN_CLOUDY_N,
                           older$P_GENDER) |>
     plot()
```
